analysis.one_liner: Exempts local phone companies from federal regulation of their high-speed internet service.
analysis.headline: The Senate never acted on the bill: after its April 1999 introduction it sat in the Commerce Committee until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the 1934 Communications Act to lift federal rules from 'advanced service' — internet connections at 200 kilobits per second or faster, which at the time meant DSL over local phone lines [S3]. The incumbent local phone carriers, mainly the regional Bell companies, would no longer have to share the lines and equipment used for that service with competitors, and their broadband prices, terms, and conditions would escape FCC regulation in most situations [S2][S3]. Where the carrier was not the local incumbent in 1996, it and its affiliates could sell broadband with no federal rate regulation at all [S3]. It also removes the duty to allow competitors to resell the carrier's broadband service [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: The incumbent local exchange carriers — the regional Bell telephone companies. The bill strips away the unbundling, resale, and price rules the 1996 Telecommunications Act applied to their DSL lines, letting them price broadband freely and keep independent internet providers off their network [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Removes federal requirements that incumbent carriers share the facilities and equipment used to provide broadband with competitors, once 70% of the carrier's loops in a state are DSL-capable.

Exempts the carrier's broadband prices, terms, and conditions from FCC regulation whenever any unaffiliated provider offers competing advanced service in the area served by a single central office — and a petition for that relief is automatically approved if the FCC does not act within 30 days.

Lets a carrier and its affiliates offer broadband with no federal rate regulation in any geographic area where it was not the incumbent carrier on February 8, 1996, freeing Bell companies to enter competitors' home territories unregulated.
Eliminates the duty not to block or burden the resale of the carrier's broadband service, cutting off a channel independent internet providers used to reach customers.

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses buying high-speed internet, who would face a dominant local carrier freed from price oversight and line-sharing duties, plus the independent internet service providers that depended on selling service over the Bell companies' lines under the 1996 Act [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: It strips price regulation and line-sharing requirements from the incumbent carrier's DSL service across most of the country, so the dominant local phone company could raise broadband prices even in places where no alternative provider actually rides its lines.

It lets the carrier refuse wholesale access to, or resale of, its broadband service, cutting off the independent internet providers that had offered competing service under the 1996 Telecommunications Act's rules.

The one concession in the bill — that FCC filings of new charges take effect automatically within two days unless the FCC stops them first — would make it very hard for the agency to police pricing before customers are affected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal was encouraging broadband investment, but the mechanism in the text is almost entirely the removal of the 1996 Act's competition safeguards from the incumbent Bell companies at the moment consumer broadband demand was taking off. The measurable effects are higher pricing flexibility for one industry and reduced access for its competitors; nothing in the text ties relief to any investment commitment. On the evidence in the bill itself, the costs to consumers and competitors outweigh the claimed benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 26, 1999, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it; it died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Sam Brownback, with Sens. Don Nickles and Larry Craig, introduced the Broadband Internet Regulatory Relief Act of 1999 on April 26, 1999.
Five Republican senators cosponsored the bill.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced; the action history records no hearing, markup, or vote afterward.
The bill remained in committee until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so it never received a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the 1996 Telecommunications Act's line-sharing, resale, and price rules stayed in place for the incumbent phone carriers' broadband service — so broadband customers and the independent internet providers competing over those lines were better off than they would have been under the bill.

for.name: Sam Brownback
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor

for.name: 5 Republican cosponsors
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Don Nickles and Larry Craig

for.name: Incumbent local telephone carriers (the regional Bell companies)
for.role: Deregulation beneficiary and longtime advocate of lifting broadband sharing rules
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for exemption of advanced services from the 1996 Act's unbundling and resale obligations.

against.name: John McCain
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a hearing or markup; the record shows no committee action after referral.

against.name: Independent and competitive internet service providers
against.role: Competitors that relied on the 1996 Act's line-sharing and resale rules
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to exempt the Bell carriers' broadband from those rules during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican, and no vote ever occurred, so the chamber's partisan split on the bill was never tested.

industries.industry: Incumbent local telephone carriers (regional Bell companies)
industries.note: The bill would exempt their DSL and other advanced services from the 1996 Act's unbundling, resale, and price rules, letting them price broadband freely and keep competitors off their network. Their gain comes directly at the expense of broadband customers, who would face an unregulated dominant provider.

industries.industry: Independent and competitive internet service providers
industries.note: The bill removes the carrier's duty to allow resale and the sharing of facilities used for advanced service, the rules under which independent ISPs offered competing service. Their interest runs with consumers', since both benefit from competitors riding the incumbents' lines.
